evidence.label: A finitely generated counterexample to the Eilenberg–Ganea conjecture

headline: Claims a group of cohomological dimension two with no two-dimensional classifying space, refuting Eilenberg–Ganea.
scope: Discrete groups; ordinary cohomological and geometric dimension. The example is a Bestvina–Brady kernel of a right-angled Artin group.
plain: Two numbers measure a group: an algebraic one, cohomological dimension, and a geometric one, the smallest dimension of a space modelling it. In 1957 Eilenberg and Ganea showed they agree from three upward, and conjectured they agree at two. The paper builds a group where the algebra says two but the geometry needs three. A Lean proof checks this counterexample.
doesNot: This does not settle Whitehead's asphericity conjecture, and the group it builds is not finitely presented.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Samuel Eilenberg and Tudor Ganea, dimensions agree from three upward
scorecard.significanceWhy: The Eilenberg–Ganea conjecture is a long-standing open problem in group theory and topology.

explanation:
The construction starts from a small group with two generators, x and y, and two rules: x² = y⁵ and x² = (xy⁻¹)³. First, a quick check. Make the group commutative and write it additively. The rules become 2x − 5y = 0 and −x + 3y = 0. The matrix of these equations has determinant 2·3 − (−5)(−1) = 1. So the commutative version is trivial: the group has no abelian shadow at all.

A group can be modelled by a space. A classifying space for a group is a connected space whose loops form that group. Its universal cover must also be contractible, meaning it can shrink to a point. The geometric dimension is the least dimension of such a space. The cohomological dimension is an algebraic count. It is the length of the shortest resolution, a chain of algebraic building blocks, needed to describe the integers over the group. Algebra never exceeds geometry: the cohomological dimension is at most the geometric one[2].

Eilenberg and Ganea showed in 1957 that the two agree when the cohomological dimension is at least 3[3]. Stallings and Swan settled dimension one. The Eilenberg–Ganea conjecture asked whether dimension two also matches. In 1997, Bestvina and Brady showed that either this conjecture or Whitehead's asphericity conjecture must fail[4]. They did not say which.

The paper claims a finitely generated residually finite group G with cohomological dimension 2 and geometric dimension 3[5]. Residually finite means every non-identity element survives in some finite image. G is the kernel of a height map on a right-angled Artin group. That group has one generator per vertex of a triangulated space, with commuting rules along edges. The obstacle is that a two-dimensional model with no holes in homology need not be contractible[6]. So ruling out one model does not rule out all of them. The paper instead tests every possible two-dimensional model at once. It uses labels in SU(2), the unit quaternions, attached to edges. Any two-dimensional model would force small labels that are flat on triangles to have trivial loop products[7]. The paper then builds small labels that are flat on every triangle but have a non-trivial product around some loop[8]. A key estimate is that commutators of labels near 1 are tiny[9]. Take the unit quaternions a = cos 0.1 + i sin 0.1 and b = cos 0.1 + j sin 0.1. Each is about 0.0999 from 1. Their commutator gap ab − ba is about 0.0199, under the bound 2·0.0999·0.0999 ≈ 0.0200. The group is not finitely presented[10].

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has a formal proof of the counterexample. It covers a finitely generated residually finite group of cohomological dimension two with a three-dimensional classifying space and no two-dimensional one. No specialist review of the paper has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if it holds, and the counterexample has a Lean proof. It leaves Whitehead's conjecture open. No specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: A connected space whose loops form the given group and whose universal cover can be shrunk to a point.
The smallest dimension of a classifying space for the group.
The length of the shortest projective resolution of the integers over the group; an algebraic measure of size.
Able to be shrunk continuously to a single point.
Every non-identity element stays non-identity in some finite image of the group.
A group with one generator per vertex of a graph, where two generators commute exactly when their vertices are joined.
The group of unit quaternions, which describes rotations in three dimensions.
